Understanding Database Replication

Replication copies data from a primary database to one or more replicas so that reads can scale out and failures can be survived. The fundamental trade-off is between consistency and availability: synchronous replication keeps replicas identical at the cost of write latency, while asynchronous replication accepts a replication lag in exchange for faster writes.

Single-leader replication is the most common arrangement. All writes go to the leader, which streams a log of changes to its followers. Followers apply the log in order, which makes them consistent with the leader eventually, and makes failover a matter of promoting the most up-to-date follower.

Multi-leader and leaderless designs relax the single point of write in exchange for conflict resolution complexity. Conflict-free replicated data types and last-writer-wins timestamps are two common resolution strategies, each with sharp edges that deserve careful evaluation before adoption.
